question: PAT Rs 800cr, CFO Rs 350cr. CFO/PAT ratio is:
before: 350/800 = 0.44x. Below 0.8x threshold -- concerning. Only 44% of profit converted to cash. 56% locked in receivables/inventory or indicates manipulation. Satyam-era levels warrant forensic analysis.
after:
Formula: CFO/PAT ratio = Operating Cash Flow ÷ Net Profit After Tax, where CFO = cash generated from operations, PAT = net profit after tax. This ratio measures what fraction of reported profit is converted into actual cash.

Step-by-step: CFO/PAT ratio = 350 ÷ 800 = 0.44x

Result: 0.44x

Why this is correct: A CFO/PAT ratio of 0.44x means only 44% of reported profit converted into operating cash flow. This falls well below the 0.8x–1.0x benchmark considered healthy. Ratios this low signal either legitimate working capital build (receivables/inventory rising faster than sales) or earnings quality issues including potential revenue recognition manipulation.

Why the others are wrong: Option A (2.29x -- excellent) inverts the division (800 ÷ 350) and misses the core insight that high CFO/PAT ratios require both strong cash generation and modest earnings. Option C (0.44x -- excellent) calculates the ratio correctly but mischaracterises 0.44x as excellent when it is materially concerning and below industry norms. Option D (2.29x -- concerning) combines the inverted calculation with the correct risk label, creating internal contradiction.

Intuition: Equity analysts use the CFO/PAT ratio as a first-pass earnings quality filter. When reported profits consistently exceed cash inflows, decompose the gap into legitimate working capital needs versus red flags in receivables ageing, inventory turnover, or deferred revenue accounting. A 0.44x ratio demands investigation into the income statement before taking headline earnings at face value.
